summary: This design note from Rohan Kapoor to Meera Iyer covers a severe lunch-hour traffic spike on the ordering API. It claims that request rates jump from 40 to about 900 per minute on weekdays, which can be easily disrupted by unconstrained clients. Furthermore, it asserts that a single poorly written polling script previously monopolized connections and can starve other students of lunch queues due to the current lack of limits. This section discusses the requirements for a rate limiting system to protect clients from one another while allowing normal student orders to proceed seamlessly. It claims that rapid users should not experience noticeable delays. Additionally, it claims that because the system uses two application instances behind a load balancer, in-memory counters are insufficient and would double the intended rate limit. The section compares three rate limiting algorithms: a fixed window, a sliding window log, and a token bucket. It notes the flaws of the first two, specifically boundary bursts in fixed windows and excessive memory use in sliding logs. Finally, it claims that the token bucket approach is best because it efficiently allows short bursts that match actual user behavior. This section covers the rate limiting rules for API clients based on their authentication status. It claims that signed-in users receive a twenty-token bucket refilled every three seconds, whereas anonymous clients share a ten-token bucket per IP address. Furthermore, it claims that reading the menu costs one token, placing an order costs five tokens, and exhausted clients receive a 429 response with a Retry-After header. This section covers a Redis-based user management approach utilizing one key per user and an atomic Lua script for operations. It claims that this method ensures reading, refilling, and spending happen in a single step. Additionally, it claims that keys expire after an hour of inactivity so memory usage scales with active users rather than total accounts.

Last term one badly behaved client slowed lunch ordering for everyone. Design a rate limiter for the
               canteen ordering API. Say which algorithm you chose and what you rejected, give real numbers, and say what
               happens when the limiter's own storage is down. Measure it under the lunch peak before you hand it in.

<<<SOURCE 2 3fa0ad8c7c99>>>
from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "When Redis is down", page 3
The limiter fails open: if Redis cannot be reached within 50 milliseconds, the request is allowed and a counter is incremented for the dashboard. Refusing every order because the limiter is broken would turn a small outage into a total one. The cost is that during a Redis outage nothing is limited, which I think is the right way round.
<<<END SOURCE 2 3fa0ad8c7c99>>>

<<<SOURCE 3 3fa0ad8c7c99>>>
from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "What I tested", page 3
A k6 script ran the lunch peak against a staging copy: 900 requests a minute from 300 virtual students, plus one client polling every 200 milliseconds. Without the limiter the p95 for placing an order was 2.4 seconds. With it, the polling client was refused about 94 per cent of the time and the p95 for everyone else came down to 310 milliseconds. No ordinary student in the test was ever refused.
<<<END SOURCE 3 3fa0ad8c7c99>>>

<<<SOURCE 4 3fa0ad8c7c99>>>
from: file rate-limiter-design.pdf, attached to Hand-in: Design rate limiting for the ordering API, section "What a limit has to do", page 1
It should stop one client hurting the others without refusing a student who is placing a normal order. A person tapping quickly should never notice it. It has to work across the two application instances behind the load balancer, so a counter in process memory is not enough: each instance would allow the full rate and the real limit would double whenever we scale.
<<<END SOURCE 4 3fa0ad8c7c99>>>

The limiter fails open: if Redis cannot be reached within 50 milliseconds, the request is allowed and a counter is incremented for the dashboard. Refusing every order because the limiter is broken would turn a small outage into a total one. The cost is that during a Redis outage nothing is limited, which I think is the right way round.
